files.n: Pocock steers with skills and prompts; Kun builds deterministic machinery
body: Pocock's repo steers the agent with small skills and grilling prompts, while Kun Chen's repos put the exact steps in scripts and gates the agent cannot skip.

Evidence: - "My agent skills that I use every day to do real engineering - not vibe coding." [Matt Pocock]
- "These skills are designed to be small, easy to adapt, and composable." [Matt Pocock]
- "Approaches like GSD, BMAD, and Spec-Kit try to help by owning the process. But while doing so, they take away your control and make bugs in the process hard to resolve." [Matt Pocock]
- "getting the agent to ask you detailed questions about what you're building" [Matt Pocock]
- "Logic that can be exact lives in deterministic scripts; work that requires understanding lives in an agent; the two never mix." [Kun Chen]
- "A denied name is removed from the model's schema entirely." [Kun Chen]
- "This is removal, not interception, and it is strictly stronger than any hook." [Kun Chen]
- "The initial change reaches the configured push target only after every local gate is green." [Kun Chen]
- "He prefers deterministic harnesses for repeated long-running loops instead of asking one context window to remember everything." [Kun Chen]

Source: Matt Pocock, skills repo README (https://github.com/mattpocock/skills (README.md), retrieved 2026-10-17); Kun Chen, firstmate VISION.md (https://github.com/kunchenguid/firstmate/blob/main/VISION.md, retrieved 2026-10-17); Kun Chen, firstmate docs/subagent-guard.md (https://github.com/kunchenguid/firstmate/blob/main/docs/subagent-guard.md, retrieved 2026-10-17); Kun Chen, no-mistakes README (https://github.com/kunchenguid/no-mistakes (README.md), retrieved 2026-10-17); Kun Chen, kun repo OPINIONS.md (a map of his views inferred from public posts and talks, not his own first-person text) (https://github.com/kunchenguid/kun/blob/main/OPINIONS.md, retrieved 2026-10-17)

body: Agent context is best delivered in five numbered layers, each read only when needed — prevention, not compression.
Evidence: "Agents read down five layers and stop when they have what they need." (ICM README)
Source: RinDig/Interpretable-Context-Methodology (arXiv:2603.16021)

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

body: The ergonomics of the tools you hand an agent dominate its cost and quality; AXI's ten principles (TOON output, minimal schemas, truncation, aggregates) beat MCP on tokens and latency.
Evidence: "GitHub MCP server will cost you to spend three times more on token cost, and more than double the latency compared to using the CLI... axi... lowest cost but highest success rate."
Source: Kun Chen, "Agent Engineering Workflow" (the importance of agent ergonomics)

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

files.n: A second brain is a context layer
body: A second brain is not a notes pile; it is a context layer — organized information built to feed context to an AI.
Evidence: "The whole idea anytime you hear a second brain at its core is just a layer to feed context to your AI. My method is a way of organizing that context layer."
Source: Jake Van Clief, "Second Brain" talk (04:35)

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

body:
Plain-file notes (an LLMwiki) stay the default memory until roughly a hundred
sources; move to RAG only when search and scale demand it, never by default.

Evidence: "It says plain files work up to about a hundred sources, which gives your
non-technical friends a real number." The second brain (62 notes) is the working
instance; nothing here needs a database yet.
Source: Captain, Troupe session 2026-10-22 ("Folders to RAG" in the Knowledge Universe)

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

files.n: ICM: the routing table is the core pattern
body: The most important thing in the entry file is a short explicit table — for this task, go to this workspace, read these files, maybe use these skills — and a rule that the agent reports which files it actually used, because a file's existence or name never guarantees it was read.

Evidence: "This is the most important pattern in the whole system… a simple table that tells the AI: for this task, read these files, skip those files, you might need these skills." Mistake 2 in 3.3: "The routing is implicit." 4.4: "A file called CONTEXT.md needs an instruction to read it; the filename alone is not a promise of automatic loading." Every Module 4 prompt ends with "tell me which source you used."
Source: Clief Notes Foundation 0.2, 3.3 (mistake 2), 4.4, 4.5

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

files.n: ICM: storage is not active context, and context is not authority
files.line: wiki note · icm, context, memory, security
body: A file on disk, a saved chat or a project folder is storage; only what is read or supplied for this request is context. Inside the context, instructions and source material sit side by side but do not carry equal authority — which is exactly why prompt injection exists and why a document must be treated as evidence, not permission.

Evidence: "Saved history and current context are different: material on disk or in a previous chat is not necessarily included in this request." "Their presence in context does not give them the same authority or turn every sentence into executable code." Memory hierarchy analogy: weights (fixed in inference), context window (RAM), system instructions, retrieved context (disk→RAM on demand), persistent memory (across sessions).
Source: Clief Notes Foundation 2.3 "How a 1953 Word Game Explains AI Memory"

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

body: The always-loaded global memory file must stay tiny because it is loaded into every session's system prompt and silently burns tokens.
Evidence: "There is only 27 lines. Because everything in this file gets loaded into the system prompt of every single agent session across all our projects."
Source: Kun Chen, "Agent Engineering Workflow" (global memory file)

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

files.n: Mini brains, not one brain of everything
body: Build many small, per-workflow brains, each bespoke to one high-value operation, instead of one brain of everything.
Evidence: "I actually make multiple second brains based on workflows, not based on everything I'm doing."
Source: Jake Van Clief, "Second Brain" talk (27:02, 11:10)

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

body: Do not let the model decide what is important; encode importance in the folder structure, which the model then follows.
Evidence: "The structure forces what is important... letting the AI decide what is important is what you shouldn't be doing."
Source: Jake Van Clief, "Second Brain" talk (31:09)

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

body: You don't need the best model for everything; efficient models do most work, and the strongest is reserved for the hard parts.
Evidence: "a lot of the time we try to use the best model possible for everything... you actually can get a lot out of these more efficient models."
Source: Kun Chen, "Full Stack App" video (intro)

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

body: Start bug fixes by reproducing the bug end-to-end as the user experiences it, not with unit tests.

Evidence: "always starts with reproducing the bug in an end to end setting... AI models today by default like to write unit tests, which are often not sufficient and not really covering the product behaviors we want to guard."
Source: Kun Chen, "Agent Engineering Workflow" (global memory rule)

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

files.n: Build with a human in the loop
body: Design systems assuming a human is in the loop; the human's abstraction is the efficient part, so amplify it rather than replace it.
Evidence: "You want to build your systems with the understanding that a human is in the loop... The human is very good at abstracting."
Source: Jake Van Clief, "Second Brain" talk (27:13)

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

files.n: Kun Chen's agent policy (a distilled self)
body: Kun's shared AGENTS.md is a concrete distilled operating policy — six rules that let any agent act with his judgment.

Evidence: "Verify before claiming... Prefer the smallest change... Do not silently revert a deliberate decision... Ask before anything destructive... Never commit secrets... Report what changed, what was verified, and what is still open."
Source: kunchenguid/dotfiles, home/AGENTS.md (this repo)

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

files.n: Popular skills are not good skills
body: Skill popularity is not quality; some widely-shared skills make agents slower and worse, so only install skills with rigorous published evaluations.
Evidence: "the agent will use 5% more tokens while making the results worse... being popular is not the same as actually being good."
Source: Kun Chen, "Agent Engineering Workflow" (how skills may hurt)

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

body: Skills load only a tiny description into the system prompt; the full body is read only when the agent decides it needs the skill.

Evidence: "when your agent starts, it only loads this tiny description field from your skills into the system prompt... only when it actually decides that it needs to use a certain skill, it will then reads the rest of this file."
Source: Kun Chen, "Agent Engineering Workflow" (using skills)

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

body: A skill and an ICM are both frozen conversations — real dialogue crystallized into a file that can be replayed.
Evidence: "A skill is technically a frozen conversation, a frozen workflow. An ICM is a frozen conversation."
Source: Jake Van Clief, "Second Brain" talk (14:40)

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

body: ADHD mode puts the key point first, in bold, then gives one idea per line, short lists and one clear next step.
Evidence: The rules are a reading layout for people who scan: the answer is in the first line, nothing important hides in a long paragraph, and the reply ends with what to do now.
Source: EA-bot talk modes, written for this site

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

body: Caveman mode answers in as few words as possible, with no filler, no greetings and no repeats of the question.
Evidence: The rule is to keep only the words that carry meaning. Fewer words also means fewer tokens to read and pay for.
Source: EA-bot talk modes, written for this site

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

body: STE100 mode writes in Simplified Technical English: short sentences, active voice, and one meaning for each word.

Evidence: ASD-STE100 is a controlled language first written for aircraft maintenance texts. It limits sentence length, asks for one instruction per sentence, and uses a dictionary where each approved word has one meaning.
Source: EA-bot talk modes, after ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

body: The endgame is a first mate — one agent you talk to that dispatches, supervises, and validates a crew across worktrees, so you focus on direction.
Evidence: "I needed a first mate, someone I can talk to as a captain that will carry out all my directions and manage all the crewmates."
Source: Kun Chen, "Agent Engineering Workflow" (first mate)

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

body: Manual git worktrees become unmanaged debt; a pool that reuses idle worktrees frees you from tracking them.
Evidence: "So this work tree basically becomes a debt... Treehouse... will try to reuse one of the idle work trees instead of creating a brand new one."
Source: Kun Chen, "Agent Engineering Workflow" (parallel worktrees)

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

body: Do not review diffs by hand (you become the bottleneck); run changes through an automated pipeline and apply judgment only at the PR, sized by risk.
Evidence: "in order to really scale ourselves with AI, we have to think of ourselves more as an engineering manager... I sense the change into a pipeline I built called No Mistakes."
Source: Kun Chen, "Agent Engineering Workflow" (validating code changes)

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

body: Autonomous overnight loops are safe when given precise caps and a verifiable objective; otherwise they can burn the weekly quota.
Evidence: "give it an objective and it will keep going until it meets some stop condition... I can set a token cap or iteration cap or stop condition more precisely."
Source: Kun Chen, "Agent Engineering Workflow" (long running tasks)

links.label: Read the public copy of this note

body: Context compaction is now an implementation detail; rely on server-side compaction and let the agent keep going across long sessions.

Evidence: "compaction... is really becoming an implementation detail that most people should not worry about anymore. Just let the agent run, let the agent compact when needed and it will just keep going."
Source: Kun Chen, "Full Stack App" video (compaction)

On the Core logic page, Claude Code, OpenCode and Pi lack a gate like this; Omnigent and ICM do the job another way.

body: The map holds house rules, a "who does what" list, and a routing table. The routing table says: for this kind of task, go to this folder and read these files first.
Scouts run a plain-English checker on their report before they say "done". It flags long sentences and vague words. It is one of the owner's two additions on top of upstream Firstmate.
/stow (upstream Firstmate) files durable facts into a curated learnings file, with decay tiers. Status on the Memory page: designed, not proven.
A guard. A script registers the pull request and its head commit, and arms a merge poll. The state comes from the forge. It does not come from the worker's message. A draft pull request is refused.
A short list of terms that must never leave the owner's machine. The build step for this page drops any note line that holds one of them, and also any line with a local path, an email or a user name.

A skill that interviews the owner until the intent is written down in their own words. The idea is from Matt Pocock's skills, which get the agent to ask detailed questions about what you are building.
The interactive Skill map and Harness flow map use the map shell from super-board by EricTechPro (MIT).
A framework from Jay E (RoboNuggets) that splits an agent workspace into four layers: Applications, Routines, Memory, Skills.

skills.desc: An upstream skill. It tells a new session how to read the start-up digest and recover.
An upstream skill. It explains each diagnostic line the start-up check can print.
An upstream skill. It holds the steps for project intake, so the supervisor does not guess them.
An upstream skill. It sets how the supervisor reasons about a fault before it starts work.

An upstream skill. It builds a digest of the supervisor's own state: what waits on the owner, what runs, what is next.

Status: not proven. It was not run for this site.
An upstream skill. It recaps visible session events and guides the owner through decisions nobody has answered yet.
An upstream skill. It decides which agent profile takes the task when a rule names several.
Every task starts as a written brief: the intent, the spec, the rules and a definition of done. A worker does one task and nothing outside the brief.
An upstream skill. It holds what differs between agent tools when a worker is started, resumed or stopped.

A guard. Each worker gets its own git worktree and its own status file. It works in that copy, not in the owner's main one.

Upstream runs each worker as a normal agent session in a visible terminal window. It does not use a tool's built-in sub-agents.

Evidence: this site was built by one such worker.
A lane, not a skill. A scout finds facts. Its output is a written report. It pushes nothing. Its worktree is thrown away after.
A lane, not a skill. A ship changes code. Its output is a pull request or a local merge. The owner says when it merges.

A lane, not a skill. Upstream describes an optional second mate: an ordinary direct report that runs from its own isolated home, on this machine or on another host.

Status: not proven. This site reports no run of one.
An upstream skill. It holds the steps for a second mate's home, from seeding to retirement.
skills.when: set up or retire a mate's home

skills.desc: An upstream skill. It tells the supervisor how to find out why a worker stopped and how to steer it.
An upstream skill. It covers sources that raise a wake when a set condition becomes true.
An upstream skill. The supervisor takes an away posture and shows a return brief when the owner is back.
An upstream skill. It cuts routine wake turns while the owner is present. Unlike /afk, ordinary chat does not end it. Only /quiet off does.

A guard. A hook is a script the tool must run. Three parts:

1. Directory change. Upstream's cd-guard stops a command that changes directory in an unsafe way (docs/cd-guard.md). Designed upstream.
2. Shell file writes. The owner's hook blocks heredoc-to-file, tee and sed -i. It blocked commands in a worker's own session. Working.
3. Secret prints. The owner's hook blocks a command that would print a secret. Installed. Not triggered in a recorded test.
skills.when: block a command before it runs

skills.desc: An upstream skill. It sets what the supervisor does before it treats a scout's work as finished.
An upstream skill (see docs/captain-hold-lifecycle.md). An owner decision is a task that waits for the owner. A worker does not close a task while such a question is open.

A guard, and the owner's own addition to a private fork. It is not upstream.

A small program checks the scout's report for Simplified Technical English (STE100-style) rules. It flags long sentences and vague words. The scout does not grade itself.

Evidence: commit f33019a6 (2026-10-28). It makes one test fail on purpose (T6). See Testing in public.

An upstream skill. A pre-push gate (no-mistakes) validates the change before it goes out. The supervisor watches that run.

Status: designed, not proven. The full ship path with the gate was not run for this site.
An upstream skill. It is the single owner of the policy for findings that ask the user.

An upstream skill. It runs the landing of a ship's work. A worker's ready signal must name a head that is pushed, not one that exists only in its disposable copy. The supervisor then registers the pull request and tells the owner the full URL.

A guard. A script registers the pull request and its head commit, and arms a merge poll. The state comes from the forge. It does not come from the worker's message. A draft pull request is refused. A ready signal whose commit is not pushed is blocked.
skills.when: ask the forge, not the worker

skills.desc: A guard. The owner decides here. Only the owner holds the level that merges. The worker opens the pull request and stops. Upstream says an owner instruction to merge is explicit authority.

A guard. The supervisor tears down a ship's copy only after landing is confirmed. If the teardown refuses because of uncommitted or unlanded work, that is a stop-and-look result. Nobody forces it without the owner's say.
A hook reminds the agent to write a short session note: goals, decisions, and where the agent went its own way. Installed. It works in one tool only, on the exact words.

A tool (backpass) reads the notes and proposes edits to the instruction files. It never writes them.

Status: runs daily; proposes rule edits; the owner approves (as of 2026-11-02).
The owner decides here. The owner reads each proposal and applies it or not. Facts enter long-term memory only after review.
One plain-text rules file that every agent reads, plus per-project files. A reviewed rule lands here. This closes the loop: the next task's Intake starts from these files.

An upstream skill. It sweeps the session for durable knowledge and files it.

Status: designed, not proven. Nothing starts it before auto-compaction. It was not exercised recently.
An upstream skill. It updates a running Firstmate and its second mates to the latest source.
An upstream skill that is only a table: each agent-only skill and the exact event that must load it.
An upstream skill. It says where Firstmate keeps its home, config, data, state and project folders.
skills.when: find a config or state path

skills.desc: Planned lane. Not built. Nothing here is proven. It would handle text and calls. Each message or call goes out only with the owner's word.
Planned lane. Not built. Nothing here is proven. It would plan the day from mail and calendar, voice first. It proposes. The owner decides.
Planned lane. Not built. Nothing here is proven. It would help with groceries, house help and stock. Nothing is ordered or booked without the owner's word.
Planned lane. Not built. Nothing here is proven. It would run a pipeline for short video and writing. It drafts. Nothing is published without the owner's word.
Planned lane. Not built. Nothing here is proven. It would score trade setups for a human, who places every trade.
